issues.issue: Does IRPA s.197 terminate a stayed appeal where the deportation rests on a s.64 offence but the breach is not a s.68(4) offence?
issues.applicant_position: Minister says Hyde's appeal was terminated by s.197 because his deportation rested on a s.64 offence; s.68(4) need not also apply.
issues.respondent_position: Hyde says s.197 requires both s.64 and s.68(4) to apply to his facts, so his appeal continues.
issues.result_quote: In my respectful opinion, the Applications Judge erred in his interpretation of section 197.

issues.issue: Does the word 'and' in s.197 (and the French text) require both s.64 and s.68(4) to apply to the facts?
issues.applicant_position: Minister says either provision suffices; the French text has no 'and' and reads s.68(4) as applying where s.64 does not.
issues.result_quote: The sense of this is that, if section 64 does not apply to a particular appellant, subsection 68(4) does.

issues.issue: Does the threshold argument (s.197 applies only if the deportation offence is a s.64 offence) succeed?
issues.applicant_position: Threshold reading would wrongly overrule Singh and produce an anomaly between pre- and post-IRPA appellants; the Minister's reading should prevail.
issues.respondent_position: Section 64 sets a threshold, so s.197 never applies to sentences under two years; Hyde's threshold reading should be accepted.
issues.result_quote: Indeed, such a result would be inconsistent with the statutory purpose of these sections discussed below.

issues.issue: Do the statutory scheme and legislative purpose support the Minister's reading of s.197?
issues.applicant_position: Scheme and purpose (serious criminality, removal of permanent residents) support terminating the appeal on any breach of the stay.
issues.result_quote: A consideration of legislative purpose thus also bolsters the interpretation of section 197 adopted in Bautista and Carbonara.
